title: Pricing by hours per project for Lawn and turf care
audience: Lawn and turf owners and supervisors who write quotes for mowing rounds and one-off lawn jobs, and need a price that covers cost and earns a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the owner's own figures
Estimate visit and job hours for a lawn, including set-up, travel and checking time
Build a lawn quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instruction.body: A mowing round is a set of visits, each with the same tasks. Hours make the cost of each visit visible, so you can see what a fortnightly plan earns and what a larger or slope-heavy lawn costs to keep. Do not price a lawn from its area alone. A 150 m² lawn with trees, slopes and tight edges can take more crew-hours than an open lawn of the same size.

instruction.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Divide the year's total cost of running the round by its chargeable hours. Include wages with on-costs such as leave and superannuation (business.gov.au, updated 1 October 2026), mower and trimmer running costs, fuel, blades and line, the vehicle, insurance, administration and premises. Use chargeable hours, not paid hours. If you pay for 40 hours and 30 are spent on client lawns, the cost per productive hour is higher than the wage. Check which award or agreement applies to each worker before using any wage figure. This lesson does not state pay rates.

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours
instruction.body: Break each visit into mowing, edging, blowing, travel between sites, set-up and a check of the lawn. Estimate each task at a standard speed for each size band, using your own log. Add set-up, pack-down and travel as named lines. Add a set allowance for delays outside your control, such as wet ground, late access and staff absence. Xero suggests 10 to 20 per cent for unexpected work (Xero Australia, 3 September 2026), but size your own allowance from your records. Back-cost past jobs by comparing quoted and actual labour before you rely on any standard time (Carters Trade Leader, 1 October 2025; New Zealand source, method only).

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the crew hours by the cost per productive hour to get the job cost. Add a margin that reflects your target and the risk, such as a steep bank or a wet site. Then apply the minimum charge. Use the Melbourne cost guide as a market check, not as a cost. It lists medium lawns (100 to 250 m²) at $68, $105 and $160 per visit as one-off jobs, and at $63, $79 and $125 per visit on a fortnightly plan, all GST included (What's the Damage, updated November 2026). Compare like with like: confirm whether your quote includes GST before comparing it with these figures.

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: A quote states the scope, the hours or price basis, the exclusions (for example, garden beds, hard-edge trimming or clippings removal if these are not included), what the client must provide (gate access, water, pets) and how long the quote is valid. Do not show the internal cost per hour to the client unless your policy says to. Re-quote when the scope changes. Where a client asks for a timed watering run, state that a Victorian watering system may run only between 6 pm and 10 am, and that the client controls the timer.

instruction.heading: Review your estimates
instruction.body: Compare estimated and actual hours for at least the first ten jobs of each type. If the variance is consistently above an agreed threshold, change the standard time, the margin or the scope rules. A method is finished when actual hours match quoted hours closely enough for the round to make money.

procedure: Gather the year's total business costs and the productive hours achieved in the same period.
Divide total costs by productive hours to get the cost per productive hour.
Break each lawn visit into tasks and estimate each task time as a range by lawn size band.
Add set-up, pack-down, travel and checking time as named lines.
Multiply the crew hours by the cost per productive hour, add the delay allowance, then apply the margin.
Apply the materials policy and the minimum charge.
Write the quote with scope, hours basis, exclusions, client inputs, GST status and validity.
Record actual hours after each job and compare them with the estimate.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not market rates. A 150 m² medium lawn on a fortnightly round needs 1.5 crew-hours for mowing, edging and blowing, plus 0.25 hours for travel and set-up. The owner's cost per productive hour is $55 (illustrative). The target margin on price is 25 per cent (illustrative).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the cost of one visit, what is the price with a 25 per cent margin on price, and what changes if a 10 per cent delay allowance is added to the hours?
workedExamples.reasoning: The crew-hours total 1.75, so the cost is 1.75 multiplied by $55, which is $96.25. A 25 per cent margin on price means the price is the cost divided by 0.75, which gives $128.33. The Melbourne fortnightly medium-lawn range is $63 to $125 per visit, GST included, so this price sits above the typical plan figure. Before choosing a price, the owner checks the standard mowing time, the scope and the GST basis. With a 10 per cent delay allowance, the hours become 1.925, the cost $105.88 and the price $141.17. The owner bills that allowance only if the quote's terms allow it.

equipmentAndPpe: Time log for each visit, with estimated and actual columns
Measuring tape or laser measure for lawn area estimates

commonErrors.error: Pricing from the hourly wage alone
commonErrors.prevention: Include on-costs, vehicle, mower and trimmer running costs, consumables, insurance and administration in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting paid hours as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use chargeable hours only when calculating the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out travel, set-up and checking time
commonErrors.prevention: Add these as named lines on every estimate.
List what is excluded, what the client provides, and the access and watering assumptions.

commonErrors.error: Never comparing estimates with actual hours
commonErrors.prevention: Record actual hours after each job and review the variance monthly.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Pricing guidance only. The Australian Consumer Law applies to pricing statements, and misleading statements about prices are prohibited (ACCC, 15 July 2026). State and territory fair trading rules also apply and differ, so check the rules for your state.

Pay rates, allowances and on-costs for employees may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. Check which one applies to each worker before using any cost figure. Coverage for lawn workers is not confirmed in this lesson.
Tax and superannuation treatment of the owner's own pay is not covered here. Confirm it with a registered tax agent.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows scope, hours or price basis, exclusions, client inputs, GST status and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the owner's own records and dated.
Actual hours are recorded for at least the first ten jobs of each type and compared with the estimate.
No quote is issued without a margin decision and a minimum-charge check.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Quote showing scope, hours basis, exclusions, GST status and validity
Job time log with estimated and actual hours
summary: Hours make the work visible, so start every lawn quote from hours.
Cost per productive hour uses chargeable time, not paid time.
Travel, set-up and checking time are named lines, not hidden extras.
Compare estimates with actual hours, and change the method when they diverge.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour?
options: Only the hourly wage of the lowest-paid worker and nothing else from the accounts or the rent
The price the client pays, plus the deposit, the late fee and the crew bonus paid
The average hourly rate of competitors in the local area and their fees for the whole year
Wages with on-costs, vehicle, equipment, consumables, insurance and administration, divided by chargeable hours

knowledgeChecks.question: A lawn visit is estimated at 5 crew-hours and takes 8. What is the right response?
options: Record the actual hours, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future quotes
Leave the estimate, since the client has already paid and the crew has finished
Reduce paid hours for the crew on the next job and skip the morning break
Raise the price for this client's next job only and no one else is charged more

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a lawn quote need an exclusions list?
options: To hide the margin from the client and to keep the rates a secret from the crew
To make the quote longer and to fill up the page with more text and words for the client
To show what the price covers, so scope changes can be priced and disputes are reduced
To lower the client's expectations and to make the job seem much smaller than it is

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly cost.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.

Xero Australia, 'How to price services', https://www.xero.com/au/guides/how-to-price-services/, dated 3 September 2026. Supports: divide by billable hours, not total hours; 10 to 20 per cent allowance for unexpected work; review prices at least once a year.

Carters Trade Leader, 'Estimating how many hours a job will take: Why 83% get it wrong', https://tradeleader.carters.co.nz/trade-skills/estimating-how-many-hours-a-job-will-take-why-83-get-it-wrong/, dated 1 October 2025. New Zealand publisher; general method only. Supports: compare quoted and actual labour to correct the next estimate. Its suggestion of a 20 per cent gross margin floor is one author's view and is not used here.

What's the Damage, 'Lawn mowing cost Melbourne', https://whatsthedamage.com.au/lawn-mowing-cost-melbourne/, verified 1 November 2026, updated November 2026. Cost guide, not a regulator; GST included. Supports: medium-lawn one-off and fortnightly per-visit ranges.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: include total overheads and sales costs when checking a price.
